# Peripartum Cardiomyopathy: A Narrative Review

## Introduction and Definition

Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) is an idiopathic form of heart failure (HF) that affects previously healthy women toward the end of pregnancy or in the months following delivery. PPCM is a form of systolic heart failure with reduced left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) affecting childbearing women during pregnancy or in the early postpartum period. The condition was first codified in 2000, when a National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute and Office of Rare Diseases workshop established formal recommendations and a case definition. [1] In 2010, the Heart Failure Association (HFA) of the European Society of Cardiology (ESC) refined this definition. The 2010 ESC Working Group revised the definition of PPCM to "an idiopathic cardiomyopathy presenting with HF secondary to LV systolic dysfunction towards the end of pregnancy or in the months following delivery, where no other cause of heart failure is found." [2] A 2019 update simplified the criteria. The 2019 ESC position paper simplified the definition to three criteria: HF secondary to left ventricular systolic dysfunction with LVEF <45%, occurrence towards the end of pregnancy or in the months following delivery, and no other identifiable cause of heart failure; the left ventricle does not necessarily need to be dilated. [3] Importantly, PPCM is a diagnosis of exclusion in women presenting with HF due to LV systolic dysfunction and should be considered when no other cause is evident. [4]

## Epidemiology and Risk Factors

The reported incidence varies markedly by geography and ethnicity. PPCM occurs in approximately 1:2000 deliveries in the United States and worldwide. [5] A nationwide US analysis examined temporal trends. The reported incidence of PPCM in the United States varies widely, and the authors queried the 2004-2011 Nationwide Inpatient Sample to identify women aged 15 to 54 with the diagnosis and to analyze trends in incidence and major adverse events. [6] Recognized risk factors include African ancestry, advanced maternal age, multiparity, multiple gestation, and hypertensive disorders of pregnancy. The strongest of these is pre-eclampsia: a systematic review determined the prevalence of pre-eclampsia in women with PPCM, noting that pre-eclampsia is often cited as a risk factor and that the two conditions may share mechanisms contributing to their pathobiology. [7]

## Pathophysiology

A landmark 2007 study established a hormonal mechanism. Hilfiker-Kleiner and colleagues showed that female mice with a cardiomyocyte-specific deletion of stat3 develop PPCM, with enhanced cardiac cathepsin D expression associated with generation of a cleaved antiangiogenic and proapoptotic 16 kDa form of the nursing hormone prolactin. [8] Subsequent work refined this picture: due to increased oxidative stress, the full-length 23-kDa prolactin is cleaved into the anti-angiogenic, pro-inflammatory, pro-apoptotic 16-kDa fragment by cathepsin D and matrix metalloproteinases, and this fragment triggers the release of microRNA-146a, which has detrimental effects on cardiomyocytes. [9] A complementary "vascular" hypothesis emerged in 2012. PPCM is associated with a systemic angiogenic imbalance, accentuated by pre-eclampsia; mice that lack cardiac PGC-1α develop profound PPCM, and the PPCM is entirely rescued by pro-angiogenic therapies. [10] In humans, the placenta in late gestation secretes VEGF inhibitors like soluble FLT1 (sFLT1), accentuated by multiple gestation and pre-eclampsia, and plasma from women with PPCM contains abnormally high levels of soluble FLT1. [10]

A genetic predisposition is now well established. In 172 women with PPCM, 26 distinct rare truncating variants were identified in eight genes; their prevalence (15%) was significantly higher than in a reference population but similar to dilated cardiomyopathy cohorts, and two-thirds were in TTN, found in 10% of patients. [11] These findings indicate that PPCM shares a genetic predisposition with both familial and sporadic idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy, and truncating variants in TTN are the most prevalent genetic predisposition. [11] A larger cohort confirmed and extended this. PPCM occurs in approximately 1:2000 deliveries; the genetic underpinnings remain poorly defined, and approximately 10% of women with PPCM harbor truncating variants in TTN. [12]

## Clinical Presentation and Diagnosis

Diagnosis is frequently delayed because symptoms overlap with normal pregnancy. Delays in diagnosis may occur because the symptoms and signs of PPCM can mimic the normal findings of late pregnancy and the peripartum period. [4] Echocardiography is the cornerstone of evaluation, demonstrating reduced LVEF, with electrocardiography, cardiac MRI, and natriuretic peptides serving as adjuncts. Diagnostic criteria include LVEF <0.45 or fractional shortening <30%, and electrocardiography, MRI, endomyocardial biopsy, and cardiac catheterization aid in diagnosis and management. [13] A high index of suspicion is essential, as outlined in the 2019 ESC position statement. [14]

## Management

Standard guideline-directed HF therapy forms the foundation of treatment, with attention to drug safety in pregnancy and lactation. Disease-specific therapy targeting the prolactin pathway has been the major therapeutic advance. A randomized open-label proof-of-concept pilot study in South Africa compared standard care versus standard care plus bromocriptine for 8 weeks; significantly fewer bromocriptine patients met a composite poor-outcome endpoint, and findings suggested improved LVEF, functional class, and survival. [15] This concept was tested in a larger trial. In a multicentre trial, 63 PPCM patients with LVEF ≤35% were randomized to short-term or long-term bromocriptine in addition to standard HF therapy, which was associated with a high recovery rate and very low rate of adverse outcome in severe forms of PPCM. [16] Earlier mechanistic and clinical work confirmed that bromocriptine reduces prolactin production by dopamine agonist actions and may improve outcomes by eliminating the cleaved 16 kDa fragment, with early use shown to improve outcomes in proof-of-concept studies. [17] Anticoagulation, treatment of arrhythmias, and—in refractory cases—mechanical circulatory support or transplantation may be required. Mechanical support and transplantation might be necessary in severe cases, and targeted therapies such as intravenous immunoglobulin, pentoxifylline, and bromocriptine have shown promise in small trials but require further evaluation. [18] Contemporary care emphasizes multidisciplinary management and patient education. [19]

## Prognosis and Outcomes

Outcomes are heterogeneous, ranging from full recovery to chronic HF, transplantation, or death. The prospective North American IPAC study provided definitive contemporary data. Among 100 women followed through 1 year postpartum, most recovered, but 13% had major events or persistent severe cardiomyopathy; Black women had more LV dysfunction at presentation and follow-up, and severe LV dysfunction and greater remodeling at entry were associated with less recovery. [20] Notably, no subjects with both a baseline LVEF <0.30 and an LVEDD ≥6.0 cm recovered by 1 year, whereas 91% with both a baseline LVEF ≥0.30 and LVEDD <6.0 cm recovered. [20] The original IPAC design recognized this variability: while 50% of women experience dramatic myocardial recovery, others develop chronic cardiomyopathy and progress toward poorer outcomes including death or cardiac transplantation. [21] European registry data complement these findings. The ESC EORP registry reported the clinical presentation, management, and 6-month outcomes in women with PPCM. [22] An influential earlier study compared timing of presentation. Elkayam and colleagues described the clinical characteristics of pregnancy-associated cardiomyopathy and compared early and late presentation. [23]

## Conclusion

PPCM remains a major contributor to maternal morbidity and mortality, yet substantial progress has been made in understanding its dual hormonal-vascular and genetic pathophysiology. Recent reviews discuss the epidemiology and clinical presentation of PPCM, as well as the mechanistic basis for potential therapeutics. [24] Continued attention to early recognition, evidence-based HF therapy, disease-specific treatment, genetic evaluation [25], and structured counseling regarding breastfeeding and subsequent pregnancies [26–30] offers the best opportunity to improve outcomes for affected women.
